newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia bans street rallies for 1997 election.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia bans street rallies for 1997 election.

text.p: Indonesia has issued a new campaign rule for next year's election, banning the popular street rallies and vehicle convoys of previous campaigns, the Jakarta Post newspaper reported on Saturday.

Attorney-General Singgih was quoted as saying the regulation issued on Tuesday stated electioneering could only take the form of public assemblies, media broadcasts, leaflets and other printed matter.
"Street rallies are now entirely banned," Singgih, speaking in his capacity as head of the Inspection Board of the National Election Committee, told reporters on Friday.

The Indonesian government fears large crowds during the election campaign could spark street violence and the military has already held riot-training exercises in the streets of Jakarta in preparation for expected election flare-ups.

The report said Singgih used two different phrases for public assemblies, with the first meaning gatherings in open spaces where people could listen to speeches and the second referring to limited gatherings where talks would take place with "vote-chasers".
It was not immediately clear if popular entertainment by musical groups and celebrities, a crowd-drawing feature of past campaigns, would be allowed.
Singgih said the only material which could be delivered during the tightly controlled 27-day election campaign period was contestants' programmes based on the state ideology Pancasila.

The government has allowed only three groups, the ruling Golkar party, the Moslem-orientated United Development Party (PPP) and the Christian-Nationalist Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) to contest the poll set for May 27 next year.

In addition, he said the country would be split into six specially designated zones during the campaign period. During each day of the period, which ends five days before the poll, each political group would campaign in two areas.
The zoning is meant to prevent supporters of one political group from running into another group's supporters, thereby reducing the potential for clashes.
Singgih said according to the new rule, police would have the authority to stop an election campaign gathering should violations occur.
